title: Europe’s Age of Energy Reinvention
summary: How geopolitics and system constraints are combining to catalyze investment across the energy supply chain throughout the continent
body_markdown:
### Constrained or Catalyzed?


The challenges Europe is facing are huge and recent years have shown that progress, for example with the[energy transition](https://www.apollo.com/strategies/asset-management/real-assets/energy-transition) , is not always smoothly linear. However, history has shown that the periods of energy disruption have served as a catalyst for innovation, spurring rapid, consequential and lasting changes to energy systems and markets.


The oil crises of the 1970s exposed the vulnerabilities created by dependence on a concentrated source of energy. Profound change followed. Between 1975 and 1985, the EU added roughly 80 gigawatts of nuclear capacity. The IEA has noted that technologies including solar photovoltaics, wind and lithium-ion batteries all trace important stages of their development to the innovation response that followed the period.(8) (9)


By the early 2000s, Europe’s import dependence was accelerating as domestic oil and gas production declined. Foreign dependence increased further between 2000 and 2011, with EU energy imports rising from 46.7% to 53.8%; natural gas dependence rose from 48.9% to 67% over the same period, leaving the region more exposed to external supply shocks.(10)


Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the continent moved quickly to diversify gas supplies in particular, expanding LNG import capacity and accelerating renewable development. New floating storage and regasification units, terminals and other import infrastructure opened alternative sources of gas, while the push to strengthen energy security also accelerated investment in renewables, efficiency and the broader energy system.


Geopolitical conflicts and supply constraints have brought about such a moment in Europe again today. Between March and August 2026, following the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, the EU incurred an estimated $54 billion in additional net fossil-fuel costs relative to what pre-war markets had expected.(11) That is $54 billion absorbed by higher prices, without a corresponding increase in productive energy capacity.


Reducing exposure to future external price shocks requires more secure regional supply and, consequently, lower dependence on imported fuels. That can include efforts to increase access to domestic energy, while also getting more useful energy from each unit consumed through greater electrification and efficiency.(12)


Historical precedent suggests that periods of disruption can accelerate changes that might otherwise take much longer – if the key ingredients are in place to act as a catalyst. Grasping the opportunity presented by current geopolitical events requires a policy response and the corresponding access to capital that can support investment across a wide range of assets, technologies and risk profiles.


### Private Capital-Powered


Private markets are expected to play an important role in meeting that need, complementing governments, banks and public capital markets with long-term and flexible capital.(13) (14)


That can be particularly important for corporates pursuing projects that require significant scale, bespoke structures or financing aligned with the duration and complexity of the underlying asset: a regulated transmission network does not carry the same risks as an offshore wind development, while nuclear infrastructure has different time horizons from other forms of generation or storage. Mature infrastructure, new generation and emerging technologies each present different questions of duration, risk and return, requiring capital that can be structured accordingly.


The breadth of that opportunity is already visible in the activity of Apollo-managed funds, which over the past 24 months have committed capital across a wide spectrum of Europe’s energy system, including wind, nuclear, natural gas and grid infrastructure:


- Equity capital alongside RWE to support German electricity transmission infrastructure;
- Scaled investment across credit and equity in Ørsted’s offshore wind development;
- Long-dated financing for EDF supporting nuclear development in the UK;
- And investment alongside counterparties including bp in pipeline infrastructure moving natural gas from the Caspian Basin toward Southern Europe.(15)


The structures behind those investments differ because the counterparty needs behind them differ. EDF was seeking capital to support long-dated ownership of the Hinkley Point C nuclear project. In other cases, such as with RWE and Ørsted, counterparties may require financing for significant capital expenditure, development and construction needs or for greater balance-sheet flexibility. Private capital can be tailored to those specific requirements, including through different positions in the capital structure, investment horizons and financing formats.


That creates something of a paradox for Europe’s energy reinvention: the need is systemic, but the financing solutions are often highly bespoke. Delivering the investment the Europe requires will depend on providers of flexible capital who can operate at scale, while also dealing creatively with complexity and who are able to take a long-term view.
